title: The map of this course: math, then models, then transformers
summary: The route from a two-knob line to a language model: linear algebra, calculus and probability first, then optimization and classical models, then neural networks and backpropagation, and finally tokens, attention and a small GPT you build yourself.
llm_link: A language model runs the whole map in one pass: text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors (linear algebra), attention and layers transform them (matrices and bends), the output is a probability for every next token (probability), and training nudges the weights downhill (calculus and optimization).
key_ideas: Linear algebra: lists of numbers are arrows, and matrices are machines that move arrows. Words inside a model are arrows; layers are mostly matrices.
Calculus: the derivative tells each knob which way is downhill for the loss.
Probability: a model hands out a share of belief to every possible next word, and the loss scores those beliefs.
Optimization and classical ML come before neural networks because the big ideas (descent, overfitting) are visible there on a single plot.
Every lesson = one idea + a quiz + a code problem, and the code builds up into an autograd engine, a NumPy network and a small GPT.

quiz.q: Why does the course start with linear algebra?
options: Because it is the easiest branch of mathematics
Because words inside a model are vectors and layers are mostly matrices acting on them
Because language models store a dictionary of words
quiz.explain: Every token becomes a vector, and most of what a layer does is multiply vectors by matrices. Linear algebra is the language the rest of the course is written in.

quiz.q: What job does calculus do in training?
options: It tells each knob which direction lowers the loss
It picks the next word at random
quiz.explain: The derivative of the loss with respect to a knob says how the loss changes if you nudge that knob, so you know which way is downhill.

quiz.q: Predict the result: f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2 · x. You apply f first and then g to the number 3. What comes out?
quiz.explain: f(3) = 4, then g(4) = 8. Stacking layers in a network works the same way: each layer's output is the next layer's input, and the order matters (g first and then f would give 7).

quiz.q: Why does a course about language models need probability?
options: Because a model outputs a share of belief for every possible next token, and we need a fair way to score it
Because training data is random noise
Because probability replaces the need for calculus
It doesn't; probability is only used in statistics
quiz.explain: The model's output is a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The loss used to train LLMs (cross-entropy, lesson 3.7) scores how much belief the model put on the token that actually came next.

quiz.q: Which order matches what happens inside a language model when it reads a prompt?
options: tokens → vectors → attention and layers → probabilities for the next token
quiz.explain: Text is cut into tokens, each token becomes a vector, the vectors pass through attention and layer blocks, and the end of the stack produces a probability for every possible next token.

problems.title: Average, with a proper error
problems.prompt:
Write mean(xs) that returns the average of a list of numbers.

An empty list has no average, so in that case raise a ValueError with a helpful message. Raising an error in Python looks like raise ValueError("message"): ValueError is a class you call, not a string.

mean([2, 4, 9])   # 5.0
mean([])          # ValueError
problems.starter:
def mean(xs):
    # TODO 1: if xs is empty, raise a ValueError

    # TODO 2: return the sum divided by the number of entries
    pass

tests.name: averages a list
tests.code:
out = mean([2, 4, 9])
assert out is not None, 'mean returned None; did you forget to return?'
assert abs(out - 5) < 1e-9, f'(2 + 4 + 9) / 3 = 5, got {out}'

tests.name: raises ValueError on an empty list

hints: if len(xs) == 0: raise ValueError("mean of an empty list")

problems.title: Stack functions like layers
problems.prompt:
A network is a stack of layers: each one is a function, and each layer's output becomes the next layer's input.

Write run_stack(layers, x) that feeds x through a list of functions in order and returns the final output.

double = lambda v: 2 * v
add_one = lambda v: v + 1
run_stack([add_one, double], 3)   # double(add_one(3)) = 8
run_stack([double, add_one], 3)   # add_one(double(3)) = 7
run_stack([], 3)                  # 3 (no layers, nothing changes)

tests.name: applies layers in order
tests.code:
out = run_stack([lambda v: v + 1, lambda v: 2 * v], 3)
assert out == 8, f'add one first (3 -> 4), then double (4 -> 8); got {out}'

tests.name: order matters
tests.code:
out = run_stack([lambda v: 2 * v, lambda v: v + 1], 3)
assert out == 7, f'double first (3 -> 6), then add one (6 -> 7); got {out}. Are you applying the layers in list order?'

tests.name: no layers changes nothing
tests.code: assert run_stack([], 5) == 5, 'with an empty stack the input should come back unchanged'

tests.name: many layers
tests.code:
out = run_stack([lambda v: v + 1] * 10, 0)
assert out == 10, f'ten add-one layers on 0 should give 10, got {out}. Each layer must receive the previous output, not the original x.'

hints: for layer in layers: x = layer(x)

problems.title: Text to numbers (a first tokenizer)
problems.prompt:
Before a model can do any arithmetic, text has to become numbers. The simplest tokenizer gives every character an id.

Write build_vocab(text) that returns a dict mapping each distinct character of text to an id, with ids 0, 1, 2, ... assigned in sorted character order. Then write encode(text, vocab) that returns the list of ids for the characters of text.

vocab = build_vocab("banana")   # {'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'n': 2}
encode("nab", vocab)            # [2, 0, 1]

tests.name: vocab of banana
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('banana')
assert v == {'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'n': 2}, f"expected {{'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'n': 2}} (distinct characters, sorted), got {v}"

tests.name: ids are 0..n-1
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('hello world')
assert sorted(v.values()) == list(range(len(v))), f'ids should be 0, 1, ..., {len(v)-1} with no gaps, got {sorted(v.values())}'
assert v[' '] == 0, 'the space sorts before letters, so it should get id 0'

tests.name: encode
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('banana')
out = encode('nab', v)
assert out == [2, 0, 1], f'n -> 2, a -> 0, b -> 1, so expected [2, 0, 1], got {out}'

tests.name: encode keeps length
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('abc')
out = encode('cabbage'[:4], v)
assert len(out) == 4, f'one id per character: expected 4 ids, got {len(out)}'

hints: for i, ch in enumerate(sorted(set(text))): vocab[ch] = i
encode is one line: [vocab[ch] for ch in text]
